cards.claim: Early layers converge to simple configurations and require less fine-tuning than later layers, motivating early freezing
cards.conditions: Deep CNN architectures (DenseNet, ResNet, VGG) on CIFAR-10/100, 100 epoch training runs
cards.effect: Theoretical justification for why freezing early layers should not severely degrade accuracy
cards.evidence: Motivational argument based on architectural observation
cards.quote: the early layers take up most of the budget, but have the fewest parameters and tend to converge to fairly simple configurations (e.g. edge detectors), suggesting that they do not require as much fine tuning as the later layers, where most of the parameters reside

cards.claim: Freeze timing should follow the learning rate schedule, with layers' learning rates annealed to zero at scheduled points
cards.conditions: Layer-wise LR scheduling using cosine annealing without restarts; DenseNet-BC (k=12, L=76), Wide ResNet (40-4), VGG-16 on CIFAR-10/100
cards.effect: Layers frozen at predetermined schedule points rather than based on convergence signals
cards.evidence: Experimental design and implementation; four scheduling variants explored (linear/cubic × scaled/unscaled)
cards.quote: FreezeOut employs cosine annealing (as proposed by ( Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017 ) ) without restarts (as used by ( Gastaldi, 2017 ) ) with a layer-wise schedule, where the first layer's learning rate is reduced to zero partway through training (at ), and each subsequent layer's learning rate is annealed to zero some set time thereafter

cards.claim: Freezing order should proceed from early to later layers progressively
cards.conditions: All tested architectures (DenseNet, Wide ResNet, VGG); CIFAR training
cards.effect: Defines the sequence of layer freezing (layer 1 first, then layer 2, etc.)
cards.evidence: Experimental implementation: cosine annealing per layer with staggered freeze points α₁, α₂, ..., αₗ
cards.quote: each subsequent layer's learning rate is annealed to zero some set time thereafter. Once a layer's learning rate reaches zero, we put it in inference mode and exclude it from all future backward passes

cards.claim: Speedup-accuracy tradeoff exists and varies by architecture; ResNets tolerate freezing better than DenseNets, which tolerate it better than VGG
cards.conditions: DenseNet (k=12, L=76): 20% speedup → 3% error increase; Wide ResNet (40-4): 20% speedup with no accuracy loss; VGG-16: no speedup
cards.effect: Up to 20% wall-clock time reduction with acceptable accuracy loss for ResNets; diminishing returns for architectures without skip connections
cards.evidence: Empirical results from 2-5 training runs per setting on CIFAR-100 (100 epochs) and CIFAR-10
cards.quote: we empirically demonstrate that FreezeOut yields savings of up to 20% wall-clock time during training with 3% loss in accuracy for DenseNets, a 20% speedup without loss of accuracy for ResNets, and no improvement for VGG networks

cards.claim: Skip connections (residual or dense) are necessary for FreezeOut to be effective; VGG architectures without skip connections show no speedup
cards.conditions: VGG-16 with BatchNorm (no skip connections) vs. Wide ResNet and DenseNet (with skip connections), same CIFAR-100 training protocol
cards.evidence: Limited experimental set on VGG using Linear Unscaled strategy
cards.quote: FreezeOut appears to be less well-suited for use in VGG, suggesting that skip connections (either dense or residual) may be an important element enabling FreezeOut to work for the other architectures we investigate

cards.claim: Frozen layers experience reduced BatchNorm computational cost (no longer computing means and variances)
cards.conditions: Frozen layers in DenseNet, ResNet, VGG during inference mode after learning rate reaches zero
cards.effect: Partial offset to per-layer speedup calculation via reduced BatchNorm overhead
cards.evidence: Computational cost analysis in speedup estimation; acknowledged in cost model
cards.quote: the cost of other operations (nonlinearities and BatchNorm), but this seems to be offset by the fact that a frozen layer's batchnorm costs are reduced (no longer having to calculate means and variances), and we find that this is generally a reliable estimate of the achieved speedups

cards.claim: Learning rate scaling (scaling initial layer-wise LR by √λᵢ) affects the speedup-accuracy tradeoff
cards.conditions: Scaled vs. unscaled variants of linear and cubic schedules on DenseNet and ResNet
cards.effect: Scaling causes each layer's learning curve to integrate to the same value (same distance traveled in weight space), affecting convergence behavior
cards.evidence: Two variants explored for each of four scheduling strategies; results shown in Figures 2-4
cards.quote: First, we consider scaling the initial layer-wise learning rate to be √λᵢ · α, where α is the base learning rate (and the learning rate of the final layer). This scaling... causes each layer's learning curve to integrate to the same value, meaning that each layer travels the same distance in the weight space

cards.claim: Cubic (non-linear) scheduling of freeze points allocates more training time to later layers than linear scheduling
cards.conditions: Cubic schedule (αᵢ³) vs. linear schedule for freeze points across DenseNet and ResNet experiments
cards.effect: Different priority allocation to layers; cubic recommended as default strategy
cards.evidence: Four scheduling strategies compared across full hyperparameter sweep
cards.quote: Second, we vary the strategy for the how αᵢ relates to the αs of the remaining layers. The simple version we explore takes the values determined by the linear scheduling rule, and cubes them with αᵢ' = αᵢ³, as shown in Figure 1 (c) and (d). This gives more priority (in terms of training time) to later layers than does the linear schedule
